# Conformance corpus

The language-independent oracle for Lido's wire formats (REQ-ARCH-060).
Every runtime — Rust, Java, C++ — reads these files and must reproduce
them byte for byte. Decisions behind the format: D-007 and D-008 in
`doc/decisions.md`.

**Expected vectors are never generated by Lido's own runtime and never
edited to make Lido pass.** If an implementation and a vector disagree,
the implementation is wrong until shown otherwise. Each case records its
provenance in `derivation`.

## Layout

```
conformance/
├── README.md                 this file
├── manifest.schema.json      JSON Schema 2020-12 for case files
├── index.json                every schema file and every case file
├── construct-coverage.json   specs.md §3 construct -> schema
├── coverage.json             specs.md §9 requirement -> cases, or an exemption (generated)
├── schemas/<name>.cddl       one construct group per file
├── schemas/evolution/<pair>/v1.cddl, v2.cddl   old and new revisions of a schema
├── cases/<kind>/<name>.json  one file per (schema, kind); kinds below
└── tools/                    check_corpus.py, cborcheck.py, test_cborcheck.py, requirements.txt
```

`index.json` lists every file explicitly (`schemas` by file name, `cases`
by path relative to `conformance/`). `check_corpus.py` fails if the list
and the tree differ in either direction, so a dropped file is a failure
rather than a smaller test run. Harnesses should start from the index.

All JSON here is UTF-8, LF, 2-space indented where expanded, with one
trailing newline (`.gitattributes` forces LF).

## Case files

```json
{
  "$schema": "../../manifest.schema.json",
  "manifest_version": 1,
  "schema": "struct_text_keys.cddl",
  "kind": "positive",
  "cases": [ … ]
}
```

`kind` is `positive`, `negative`, `noncanonical`, `encode_error` or
`evolution`; each has its own record, below.

### Positive case

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | `<schema-stem>/<case-name>`, lower snake_case. **Stable forever**: coverage files and tests in three languages cite it. |
| `root` | Name of the type in `schema` that `value` is an instance of. |
| `description` | What the case is for. |
| `requirements` | `REQ-*` IDs the case exercises. |
| `derivation` | `rfc8949-appendix-a`, `hand-encoded`, or `cbor2`. Where the bytes came from. |
| `value` | The logical value, in the value model below. |
| `cbor` | Canonical CBOR (REQ-RT-160) as lowercase hex, no prefix or separators. |
| `json` | The exact expected JSON **text**, as a JSON string: compact (REQ-RT-175), members in canonical order (REQ-RT-177). |

`json` is text rather than an embedded value so that member order and
spelling are compared byte-exactly without re-serializing through the
writer under test.

### Value model

A value is a JSON object with **exactly one member**, whose name is a type
tag. It is self-describing: reading it needs no CDDL.

| Tag | Payload |
|---|---|
| `bool` | JSON `true` / `false` |
| `uint`, `int` | decimal **string** (`"36"`, `"-7"`) |
| `f16`, `f32`, `f64` | **string**: decimal, C99 hex-float (`0x1.8p+0`), `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity` |
| `tstr` | JSON string |
| `bstr` | lowercase hex string |
| `null` | JSON `null` |
| `array` | JSON array of values |
| `map` | JSON array of `[key, value]` pairs, key tagged `tstr` or `uint`, in expected wire order |

Integers and floats are strings so no JSON parser's double handling can
alter an expected value. Choices and enumerations have no tag: a choice is
a single-entry `map` (REQ-RT-360) and an enumeration is its literal
(REQ-RT-385). An absent optional field is simply missing from `map`; an
explicit null is `{"null": null}` (REQ-RT-330).

## Negative, non-canonical and encode-error cases

Besides `positive`, three kinds exist (`evolution` is still reserved, slice
1.4). All share `id`, `root`, `description`, `requirements` and `derivation`
with the positive record. A decode input is an object `input` with exactly one
member, `cbor` (hex, possibly empty) or `json` (exact text, possibly empty).

**`negative`** — a decode that must fail. Fields `input`, `classification`,
`error`.

- `classification` is `malformed` or `schema_invalid`. **`malformed` means a
  strict generic CBOR/JSON decoder rejects the input** — not well-formed (RFC
  8949 §1.2), *or* well-formed but with text that is not UTF-8 or a map with a
  duplicate key (REQ-RT-300/315). `schema_invalid` means the input is
  well-formed and valid generic data that is simply not an instance of `root`.
  (RFC 8949 would call the former "invalid"; here the word covers both.)
- `error.kind`: for `malformed`, one of `truncated`, `trailing_data`,
  `syntax`, `invalid_utf8`, `duplicate_key`; for `schema_invalid`, one of
  `type_mismatch`, `missing_field`, `null_not_allowed`, `unknown_discriminant`,
  `invalid_choice`, `out_of_range`, `wrong_length`, `bad_key`.
- `error.path` (required for `schema_invalid`, absent for `malformed`) follows
  REQ-RT-066: `""` is the root, `items[2].price`, `[1]`, `stock[7].qty`,
  `scores["a"]`; an integer-keyed field is its decimal key. A path resolves in
  the input (for `missing_field`: its parent does and it does not).
  Optional `discriminant` (REQ-RT-380) and `constraint` (`"0..255"`, as written
  in the schema).
- **Not pinned**: error message text, byte offset, line and column. Harnesses
  compare `classification`, `error.kind` and `error.path` only.

**`noncanonical`** — an input a decoder must accept. `variance` names how it
departs from canonical form (`indefinite_length`, `unsorted_keys`,
`non_shortest_head`, `wider_float`, `non_canonical_nan`, `whitespace`,
`string_escapes`, `number_spelling`, `int_as_string`, `int_as_number`,
`base64_padding`, `member_order`, `absent_default`); `value`, `cbor`, `json`
are the canonical vector for the value the input decodes to (`json` is omitted
only when the value has no JSON form: NaN). Pairs of a map in `value` are in
canonical order even when the input is not.

**`encode_error`** — an encode that must fail in at least one encoding.
`value` is encoded; `expect.cbor` and `expect.json` are each the exact expected
output or `{"error": {"kind", "path", ...}}` with `kind` `not_representable`
(REQ-RT-210, 255) or `out_of_range` (REQ-RT-250). The other encoding, if it
succeeds, still gives exactly its output (NaN encodes to CBOR `f97e00`).

How these are confirmed: a `malformed` input must be rejected by `cborcheck`'s
well-formedness and validity analysis and, except for duplicate keys (which
`cbor2` keeps), by `cbor2` too; a `schema_invalid` input must be accepted by
both. JSON uses a strict parser. A non-canonical CBOR input must be valid,
decode to `value`, and exhibit the departure its `variance` names; a JSON one
must equal the canonical text after exactly that relaxation. What cannot be
confirmed without a CDDL validator is that a `schema_invalid` input really is
not an instance of its `root`; the path and range checks narrow that gap.

## Evolution pairs

`cases/evolution/<pair>.json` has `"pair": "<pair>"` instead of `"schema"`; the
two revisions are `schemas/evolution/<pair>/v1.cddl` (old) and `v2.cddl` (new).
Each case says what a **reader** of one revision does with the **canonical
output of a writer** of the other:

- `scenario`: one of `add_optional_field`, `add_defaulted_field`,
  `add_uint_keyed_field`, `append_array_element`, `declaration_order_independent`,
  `nested_struct_gains_field`, `unknown_value_types` (the ways specs.md §9.6
  guarantees a schema may grow; one pair each).
- `direction`: `new_to_old` (REQ-COMPAT-020/060: v1 reads v2 output; unknown map
  entries and extra trailing array elements are discarded) or `old_to_new`
  (REQ-COMPAT-010: v2 reads v1 output; absent fields are absent or defaulted).
- `input`: the writer's canonical output, `{"cbor": …}` or `{"json": …}`.
- `value`, `cbor`, `json`: the **reader's** canonical vector — what it decodes to
  and would re-emit. Discarded fields are *not* in it (REQ-COMPAT-025).
- `ignored` (`new_to_old`, required): the paths of input entries the reader
  discards. `populated` (`old_to_new`, optional): the paths the reader fills in,
  e.g. a default. Paths follow REQ-RT-066 and must be exact.

The check confirms the reader's vector is an ordinary positive vector, the input
is the writer's canonical form, and that the paths named are exactly where the
input and the reader's value differ. Not confirmed (it needs a CDDL validator):
that v2 is a purely additive extension of v1. A compatibility *non*-guarantee
(REQ-COMPAT-040) has no expected outcome and so no vectors.

## Requirement coverage

`coverage.json` maps every requirement in specs.md §9 (introduction and
§9.1–§9.8) to the ids of the cases that test it, or to an **exemption**:

```json
"REQ-RT-110": { "exempt": { "category": "build_constraint", "reason": "…", "tested_in": "slice 2.7" } }
```

- `cases` are **generated**: every case appears under each requirement in its
  own `requirements`, plus those in `implied_by_kind` (every `positive` vector
  is an encode and decode of both formats, so it covers REQ-RT-010/020/030/040/050/170).
  `check_corpus.py --write-coverage` regenerates them and keeps the
  hand-written `implied_by_kind` and `exempt` entries; the default run fails if
  the file is stale.
- A requirement with neither a case nor an exemption fails the check, so a
  requirement added to specs.md §9 stops CI until it is covered or exempted.
- An exemption needs a `category` (`api_shape`, `dependency_policy`,
  `build_constraint`, `optional_behaviour`, `configuration`, `non_guarantee`), a
  `reason`, and `tested_in` naming a slice that exists in plan.md; only
  `non_guarantee` may omit it. An exempt requirement that gains a case fails as
  a stale exemption.
- It is not `construct-coverage.json`, which answers a different question
  (specs.md §3 constructs → schemas).

## Schemas and construct coverage

`schemas/` holds sixteen small CDDL files, one construct group each, so a
failing vector names the construct that broke. `construct-coverage.json`
maps each specs.md §3 construct (ids `C-nnn`, append-only) to the schemas
(by stem) that cover it. A construct carries either a `quote` — text that
occurs in exactly one §3 bullet — or `derives_from`, naming a requirement
when §3 does not state it. A construct with no schema must say where it is
deferred (`deferred_to`). `check_corpus.py` fails if a §3 bullet is cited by
no construct, a quote is not in `specs.md`, or a schema is missing.

## How a case is verified

`check_corpus.py` re-derives every expected value with tools that share no
code with Lido (D-007 §4). For each positive case:

1. `cbor2.loads(cbor)` equals `value` — type-strict, map pairs compared in
   order, `-0.0` distinct from `0.0`;
2. `cbor2.dumps(..., canonical=True)` of that result is byte-identical to
   `cbor`;
3. `cborcheck.py`, a standard-library validator written from RFC 8949 §4.2,
   finds no violation: definite lengths, shortest heads and floats, canonical
   NaN (REQ-RT-172), and map keys strictly increasing over their *encoded*
   bytes (REQ-RT-165);
4. `json` equals the text derived from `value` by the checker's own JSON
   writer, which implements REQ-RT-175/177/178/179/200/220/230.

It also checks that every schema has a positive case file, every `root` is
defined in its schema, ids are unique, and every `requirements` entry exists
in `specs.md`. It does **not** check that `value` is a valid instance of
`root`: that needs a CDDL parser, which would be Lido code.

`derivation` records provenance. `rfc8949-appendix-a` means the hex was
transcribed from an RFC 8949 Appendix A item and the generator asserted
equality with it; `cbor2` means `cbor2` produced the bytes; `hand-encoded`
means they were written by hand. Whichever it is, checks 1–3 still apply.

`--mutation-test` replaces every byte of every `cbor` with each of the other
255 values, and every character of every `json` with a probe set (and
deletes and doubles it), and requires the check to fail each time.

## Adding a case

1. Pick the schema and the kind; open (or create) `cases/<kind>/<stem>.json`.
2. Derive the bytes from RFC 8949, by hand, or with `cbor2` — never from
   Lido. Write `value` first and let the check tell you if the bytes agree.
3. Add the file to `index.json` if it is new.
4. Run the check (below). An existing case's expected values are never edited
   to make an implementation pass.

## Checking

```
pip install --require-hashes -r conformance/tools/requirements.txt
python3 conformance/tools/check_corpus.py --check-format
python3 conformance/tools/check_corpus.py --self-test
python3 conformance/tools/check_corpus.py --mutation-test
```

The `conformance` CI job runs all three, with no Rust toolchain involved. It
is a required check (D-009).
